initial_presentation: A 13-year-old Caucasian male with mild intellectual disability, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, and constipation was transferred to our tertiary care facility due to a two-month history of difficulty swallowing and recurrent vomiting episodes. Initially, vomiting occurred only after ingesting solids, but it progressed to include liquids. Obtaining further history was challenging due to the child's intellectual disability and speech delay. Information from family members and caregivers at the psychiatric institution indicated that the boy also experienced self-induced vomiting, heartburn, and a seven-pound weight loss in one week. His medications included polyethylene glycol and ranitidine. Physical examination upon admission was unremarkable.

A 15-year-old male presented to the thoracic surgery clinic with a non-tender mass on the anterior chest wall that had been slowly enlarging over a period of 2 months. Initially, the mass was thought to be a subcutaneous abscess due to its slow growth and fluctuation upon palpation.

A two-year-old girl was referred to the Urology Department for the management of vesicoureteral reflux (VUR). She had initially experienced a urinary tract infection (UTI) before presentation at the age of two, when right hydronephrosis and VUR on the same side (Grade IV) were observed. She was born to nonconsanguineous parents as a twin at 29 weeks' gestation, with a birth weight of 2,069 g.

A 53-year-old woman presented with an asymptomatic cyst on her left vulva of uncertain duration. The initial clinical assessment suggested a vulvar abscess. There was no known history of generalized skin conditions with similar characteristics, and no associated lesions were found on the vulva or cervix. The family history was negative for dermatologic conditions involving multiple papules and nodules.

A 29-year-old pregnant woman, gravida 2, para 1, was referred to the Department of Medical Genetics and Prenatal Diagnosis Center of West China Second University Hospital. She and her spouse were non-consanguineous, with no notable medical conditions, and denied a family history of genetic diseases or a known history of neurological disorders. She was in her second pregnancy at 12 weeks with no complications and had no notable history in her first pregnancy. The firstborn, a 2-year-old girl, was born naturally at full term with a normal occipitofrontal circumference (33.5 cm) and weight (3.2 kg) at birth. During her first year of life, macrocephaly was observed, with a head circumference of 46 cm (> +3 SD) at 6 months and 48.5 cm (> +3 SD) at 8 months. At 1 year and 3 months, her head circumference increased to 53.5 cm (> +3 SD), while her height (75 cm) and weight (10 kg) were normal. The child exhibited severe motor developmental delay and low muscle tone, unable to roll over at 6 months, stand until 1 year and 6 months, or crawl and independently sit and walk until 2 years old. She often walked unsteadily and had poor motor coordination. There were no early-onset seizures, epilepsy, or spasticity before 2 years of age, and her vision and hearing functions were normal. Cognitive functions were delayed; she could say a few enunciated words but often spoke to herself unconsciously and could not understand the meaning of words, follow instructions, express her intentions, or otherwise verbally communicate. At 19 months of age, she had a motor developmental index of less than 50 and a cognitive developmental index of 52 on the Bayley Scales of Infant Development (BSID-II), corresponding to the levels of 10- and 12-month-old infants, respectively. These results indicated substantial deficits in her motor, cognitive, and language development levels outside the normal range.

A 39-year-old female presented with several months of right knee pain, swelling, and instability, especially when descending stairs. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medications provided only mild relief. She reported no night pain, systemic symptoms, or recent trauma. Her medical history included congenital hip dysplasia, and there was no family history of inflammatory diseases, bone disorders, or dysplasia. Physical examination revealed a mild antalgic gait, right knee effusion, and tenderness along the lateral joint line. A firm, palpable mass was noted on the anterolateral proximal tibia without erythema or skin ulceration. The rest of the physical examination was unremarkable.

A 10-year-old afrodescendant female child presented to the oral medicine service with a primary concern of painless gingival swelling, which was causing difficulty in chewing and aesthetic issues. The patient's mother reported no systemic health issues, chronic medication use, or complications during pregnancy and delivery. The gingival enlargement was first noticed at age 5 during deciduous dentition and intensified with the emergence of permanent teeth. The mother also mentioned that the child's father exhibited similar features, while she herself did not. The child's past medical history was unremarkable. Extraoral examination showed elevated lips, a pronounced open bite, and difficulty achieving a passive lip seal. Intraoral examination revealed generalized gingival enlargement covering nearly all maxillary and mandibular teeth, leading to problems with swallowing, speaking, and aesthetics. The gingival tissue had a rough texture, pink color, and fibrous consistency, with areas of melanic pigmentation and hyperemia at the gingival margins in the anterior vestibular region. In the palatal region, the enlargement extended toward the midline, partially obscuring the palate's depth. Teeth were displaced, with crowns partially or fully embedded in the fibrotic tissue. The gingiva was painless upon palpation. Hematological tests were normal, indicating no systemic involvement.
A 59-year-old female with no significant past medical history arrived at the emergency room presenting with fever, headache, drowsiness, and body pains for one week.

A nine-month-old girl was admitted to the hospital with symptoms of fever, cough, diarrhea (11-12 episodes daily), and failure to thrive. She was born at term via normal delivery with a birth weight of 3200 grams following an uneventful pregnancy. She is the second child of a non-consanguineous Turkish couple, with a healthy 5-year-old sister. Upon admission, her body weight was 4.7 kg (SD: -3.5), height was 62.5 cm (SD: -1.7), and head circumference was 39 cm (3rd percentile). Relative index was 71.2. Physical examination revealed pallor, thin and weak hair, and decreased subcutaneous adipose tissue. Auscultation detected rales in the middle zone of the left lung. Her abdomen was distended with prominent bowel loops, and she had umbilical and bilateral inguinal hernias. Dysmorphic features included hypertelorism, frontal bossing, triangular face, and retromicrognathia. She had complete head control but could not sit without support. Deep tendon reflexes were normoactive.

A 7-year-old male was brought to the pediatric outpatient department by his mother. He exhibited aggressive and hyperactive behavior, frequent falls from sitting and standing positions, and a loss of speech over the past five months. These symptoms progressed rapidly during the first month and then remained unchanged for the subsequent four months. Initially, he had slurred speech which worsened to difficulty in articulation. He was unable to sit or stand without support and could not express a need for food. He also had difficulty understanding and following commands. Previously, he was an active child capable of performing routine activities, with no family history of childhood seizure disorders. On general physical examination, the child had an average height and build with no dysmorphic facial features. He was restless and hyperactive in bed, restrained by his mother, with forward falling of the trunk while sitting. Vital signs were normal. Anthropometric measurements were: height 116 cm (10th-25th percentile), weight 20 kg (25th percentile), and occipitofrontal circumference (OFC) 50 cm (25th percentile). He was partly responsive to his mother with purposeless movements and no verbal response to commands. Sensory and motor examinations were normal. Cranial nerves were grossly intact. There were no cerebellar signs or nystagmus. On gait examination, he was unable to walk without support. With support, mixed movements including high stepping, jumping, and ataxic gait were observed. Systemic examination was unremarkable.
